title: Suffering calmly
hook: a carpenter's bubble, and a hymn about one who sees gold and clay the same

segments.voice: Yesterday, freedom of conscience: the ninth Guru went to Delhi for people whose thread he didn't wear. Your line was their faith, their right. Where did you make room for someone else's way? Day one thousand two hundred seventeen.

A carpenter's level is a simple tool. A little tube of liquid with one bubble trapped inside. Tilt the board one way and the bubble runs off. Tilt it the other way and it runs off again. Only when the board is true does the bubble sit still, right between the two lines. A lot of days feel like a board being tipped back and forth. Good news, and the bubble runs. Bad news, and it runs the other way. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote a hymn about a person whose bubble stays in the middle.
screen: `A TUBE, ONE BUBBLE.` → `TILT, AND IT RUNS.` → `A PERSON WHO STAYS LEVEL.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raga Sorath, paraphrased. The one who, in pain, does not take pain as pain. Who has no clinging to pleasure, and no fear. Who looks on gold as clay. Who is moved neither by slander nor by praise, and is free of greed, attachment and pride. Who stays the same in joy and in sorrow, in honor and in dishonor. In that one, the hymn says, the Lord lives. And it ends with an image: such a person blends with the Lord like water blending into water. Notice what the hymn does not say. It doesn't say the level person feels nothing. It doesn't say pain isn't real. What it keeps returning to is pairs: pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay. The trick isn't escaping one side. It's not being thrown by either side. A raise and a rejection both get met by the same steady person. That's why the carry is one word. Level. And this wasn't theory for the man who wrote it. We heard yesterday how his life ended, in Delhi. Sikh tradition remembers him meeting it calmly. A short salok of his, near the end of the Granth, says the same thing in fewer words: the one untouched by pleasure and pain, by greed, attachment and pride, is the very image of the Lord. A normal day asks for nothing like that. But the bubble still runs. A text that stings. A compliment that goes to your head. Same practice for both: notice the tilt, and let the bubble come back to the middle.
screen: `IN PAIN, NOT TAKING PAIN AS PAIN.` · `GOLD AND CLAY, PRAISE AND SLANDER.` · `WATER BLENDING INTO WATER.` · `NOT THROWN BY EITHER SIDE.` · then, large: `LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay level through one mood. Settle, and breathe. Notice the mood you're in right now. Name it plainly: tired, happy, worried, flat. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just let it be there, the way weather is there. Now picture the bubble in the level. With each breath out, let it settle a little nearer the middle. If a pleasant thought pulls you up, notice. If a heavy one pulls you down, notice. Come back to the middle. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Suffering calmly. The ninth Guru's hymn praises one who meets pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay the same, and stays level. Today's word.
Your line: level. Today, when something tips you, good or bad, say the word level once under your breath, and let the bubble come back. Day one thousand two hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, such as this one in Raga Sorath, in kirtan, and his saloks on meeting pleasure and pain alike are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

it says such a person isn't thrown by pain or pleasure, not that they feel nothing.

pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay.

fork.setup: in one morning you get a big compliment and a harsh criticism. how does the person in the ninth Guru's hymn meet them?
options: enjoy the praise, brush off the criticism.
meet both the same, without being thrown.
dwell on the criticism until it's fixed.
fork.reveal: the hymn praises one moved by neither slander nor praise, the same in joy and sorrow. in that one, it says, the Lord lives.

original.note: pain, sorrow; the hymn praises one who, in pain, does not take pain as pain.

trapdoor: what you thought: suffering calmly means hiding your pain.
what it means: not being thrown by pain or pleasure, praise or slander. staying level.
what a scholar hears: the Sorath hymn of Mahala 9 ends with water blending into water, its picture of the level person joined to the Lord.
